chapter: Lucky Roberts, Armstrong and the big-band rivalries
title: Armstrong on the Paris Blues set; the smaller-bore advice
summary: He met Armstrong only when they made Paris Blues together; Armstrong told him to use a smaller bore horn so as not to wear himself out, and Butler recalls the Hot Fives records.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Now, Louis Armstrong, he -- I didn't meet him until I made the picture with him. And he liked me and I liked him. It was a mutual thing.
When did you make the picture with him?

This was in 1967 or something, I made a picture, 'Paris Blues' with him. (1961--ed.) And he used to come and somebody." But...he told me get a smaller bore (inaudible). He told me, he says "Butler is / and swing that melody. Don't worry about it. That's what it is."

Yeah, because I was using a large-bore horn, you see. And I was popping. But he knew if I kept popping, it would wear me out. Take me out, see. So that's what he told me. He told me that. And I said, 'Pops, when that was gone, could I have it?' He says, 'Yes. That was yours.' See, Selma used to give me all my horns.
But you had heard him many times?

Well, I laid on him with joy. Sure, I heard him -- the first time I heard him when he played this 'Potato Head Blues' and 'Heebie Jeebies', well, that was it. And 'Wild Man Blues.' And it is still it. Still it. And
Well you don't have that many people playing that much cornet. I mean, that is really coronet. It's not clarinet, it's not -- it's the instrument itself. Sure, my goodness.
